summary.text: A 13-year-old girl was referred to the endodontic department in 1972 with dens invaginatus type IIIb, pulp necrosis and a chronic apical abscess of the left lateral maxillary incisor (tooth #22), with a sinus tract and periapical radiolucency. Nonsurgical root canal treatment was performed over three visits and the tooth was obturated with gutta-percha and AH26 cement; complete healing was documented at the 3-year follow-up.

In 2002 the patient returned with pain and swelling and an acute apical abscess of tooth #22, which had a post and crown with marginal defects and periapical radiolucency. Endodontic surgery used a modern protocol with an operating microscope, lidocaine with epinephrine, root-end resection and IRM root-end filling. Follow-up showed an asymptomatic tooth and complete healing in 2006.

In 2011 she returned with sensitivity, purulent exudate, a sinus tract and a chronic apical abscess; failure of the apical seal was suspected as the reason for the recurrent lesion. A second endodontic surgery used the same technique with minimal apical resection. Two years following the second surgery the tooth was asymptomatic and completely healed radiographically.

In 2021, aged 63 years, she was referred by the treating dentist for evaluation; the tooth was asymptomatic with normal periapical tissues and complete healing. She did not attend any follow-up appointments after 2021 despite multiple attempts to contact her. The interval from the reoperation to the last follow-up is stated as both 10 and 11 years.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 1.
Nonsurgical root canal treatment on tooth #22. (A) Preoperative radiograph in 1972 showing a periapical radiolucent area that extends mostly on the distal surface of the root. Note: an access cavity was present. Gutta-percha cone inserted in the sinus tract leading to the sulcus of the tooth. Three pulp cavities are visible: the distal one exposed by the access cavity, the middle one partly lined with enamel, and the mesial one is closed and present only in the apical half of the root. (B) Postoperative radiograph in 1972. Note the extruded cement and gutta-percha point beyond the apex. Mesial cavity unfilled. (C) Two-year follow-up radiograph in 1974 showing a decrease in the size of periapical radiolucency. Excess filling material settled on the distal aspect of the root. Reprinted from the article of Tagger et al. [16] with the permission of Elsevier.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 2.
Endodontic surgery on tooth #22. (A) Preoperative radiograph in 2002 showing periapical radiolucent area around the apex and distal aspect of the root. Note the excess filling material outside the root. At the time of referral, the tooth had been restored with a post and crown. Marginal defects can be seen in the final restoration. (B) Intraoperative photograph in 2002. (C) Postoperative radiograph in 2002. The apical part of the mesial cavity was prepared and filled. Excess filling material that was outside the root was removed. (D) Four-year follow-up radiograph in 2006 showing complete healing with no periapical radiolucency present.

article_limitations: Source conflict: year of the first treatment is 1972 (case description, Figure 1, Table 1) versus 1977 (discussion); the year is kept only in separate review_only facts.

Source conflict: two-year follow-up after the 2011 reoperation is dated 2012 in the Figure 3 caption and 2013 in Table 1; the interval from reoperation to last follow-up is 10 years in the Figure 4 caption and 11 years in the abstract and conclusion.
Table 1 radiographic cell for 2011 reads Normal apical tissues although the 2011 text describes a chronic apical abscess; the cell is kept literal and quarantined as review_only.
Text cites Figure 2C for the 2-year follow-up while the caption describes panel C as the 2002 postoperative radiograph.
Discussion statements about cited cases, general endodontic recommendations and success rates are not index-patient facts and were not recorded.
Figure 1 is reprinted from the earlier Tagger report; its caption names tooth #22 and the text cites it for this patient's two-year radiograph, so it is attributed to the index patient.
